title: Idempotency & Exactly-Once
subtitle: Watch a payment get retried after a lost response, and see how an idempotency key stops the customer being charged twice.
learn: Why a retry after a timeout can run the same operation twice
How an idempotency key plus a dedup table makes a request safe to repeat
Why exactly-once delivery is really at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing
How to make the dedup check and the side effect commit atomically
Where keys expire, collide, or get reused with a different payload

steps.title: Did my payment go through?
steps.body: A customer taps Pay for a $40 order. The request reaches the server and the charge succeeds, but the response is lost on a bad mobile network. The app sees a timeout. It cannot tell whether the charge happened. Retrying might charge twice; giving up might lose the order.
steps.idea: After a timeout the caller cannot distinguish 'never arrived' from 'done, but the reply was lost'.
steps.caption: One tap, one charge, one lost reply.

steps.title: The charge succeeds
steps.body: The app sends POST /charges for $40. The API writes the charge to the ledger and returns 200. So far this is the happy path, and the ledger holds one charge. Nothing in the request says 'this is the same order as before', which will matter in a moment.
steps.idea: A plain POST has no identity: the server cannot tell a repeat from a new request.
steps.caption: Ledger records one $40 charge.

steps.title: The reply is lost
steps.body: The 200 response never reaches the phone because the connection dropped. The client's timeout fires after, say, 10 seconds. From its side the request failed. Retries are the right instinct (the timeouts and retries lesson covers how to space them), but they are only safe if repeating the operation is harmless.
steps.idea: Retries turn an unreliable network into at-least-once execution, so duplicates are normal, not rare.
steps.caption: Response dropped; the client sees a timeout.

steps.title: The naive retry double-charges
steps.body: The app retries the same POST. The server has no memory of the first one, so it inserts a second $40 charge. The customer is billed $80 for one order, and a support ticket and a refund follow. At 1 million payments a day with a 0.1% timeout-then-retry rate, that is about 1,000 duplicate charges daily.
steps.idea: Without a guard, every retry of a non-idempotent operation is a potential duplicate side effect.
steps.caption: Second insert: customer billed $80.

steps.title: Add an idempotency key
steps.body: An operation is idempotent if doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once. To get that for a POST, the client generates a unique key (a random UUID) per logical action, such as one order, and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header. Every retry reuses the same key. The server can now recognise repeats.
steps.idea: The client names the intent once; the server uses that name to collapse repeats into one effect.
steps.caption: Same key on every attempt for this order.

steps.title: First attempt claims the key
steps.body: The API looks the key up in a dedup table. It is new, so the API inserts the key and the $40 charge in one database transaction, then stores the response it will return. The key column has a unique constraint, so two concurrent attempts cannot both claim it: the database lets exactly one insert win.
steps.idea: A unique constraint plus a transaction makes 'check then act' atomic; checking first in app code is a race.
steps.caption: Key and charge commit together.

steps.title: The retry is recognised
steps.body: The reply is lost again, and the app retries with the same key. The API finds the key already stored, skips the ledger entirely, and returns the saved response from the first attempt. The customer sees success, and the ledger still shows one charge. The retry cost one cheap lookup instead of a second payment.
steps.idea: A repeat returns the original result; it must not re-run the side effect.
steps.caption: Duplicate blocked; stored reply returned.

steps.title: Exactly-once is a stack of at-least-once
steps.body: The ledger then publishes a 'charge created' event to the queue. Brokers usually deliver at-least-once: if the worker crashes before acknowledging, the message comes back. Truly exactly-once delivery across a network is not achievable in general. What you build is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer, which records processed message IDs so a redelivered receipt email is skipped.
steps.idea: Exactly-once effect = at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing, with the dedup record committed alongside the effect.
steps.caption: Worker dedups redelivered events by ID.

steps.title: Edge cases that bite
steps.body: Keys are stored with a TTL, commonly 24 hours, so the table does not grow forever; a retry after that window would run again. If the same key arrives with a different amount, reject it with an error rather than guessing. If an attempt is still in progress, a concurrent retry should wait or get a 409, not start a second run. Keys should be random per action, never derived from just the user ID.
steps.idea: Scope the key per action, bind it to the request payload, expire it deliberately, and handle in-flight duplicates.
steps.caption: Key reused with a new amount is rejected.

steps.title: Safe to retry
steps.body: Networks lose replies, so callers must retry, and retries create duplicates. The client sends one key per intent. The server claims the key atomically with the effect, returns the stored result for repeats, and expires keys after a window. Consumers of at-least-once queues do the same with message IDs. That is how systems get exactly-once effects.
steps.idea: Assume duplicates will happen and make them harmless.
steps.caption: One order, one charge, however many retries.

quiz.q: A client times out waiting for a charge response and retries with no idempotency key. What is the real risk?
options: The server will reject the retry as malformed
The charge may run twice, because the first may have succeeded
The retry will always be faster
The database will deadlock
quiz.why: A timeout does not tell the client whether the first request executed. Without a key the server cannot recognise the repeat, so a successful first attempt plus a retry equals two charges.

quiz.q: Your handler does: SELECT key; if absent, charge the card, then INSERT key. Two identical requests arrive at the same moment. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, SELECT is atomic
Both see the key absent and both charge
The second request is blocked by the first automatically
The key is stored twice but only one charge occurs
quiz.why: Check-then-act is a race. Both requests can pass the SELECT before either inserts. Claim the key with a unique-constraint INSERT in the same transaction as the effect so only one can win.

quiz.q: Which statement about exactly-once delivery is most accurate?
options: Modern brokers guarantee each message is delivered exactly once over the network
It is achieved by at-least-once delivery combined with an idempotent consumer
It is achieved by disabling retries
It only matters for databases, not queues
quiz.why: A sender cannot know if a lost ack means the message was processed, so it must redeliver. Exactly-once effect comes from deduplicating by message ID on the consumer side.

quiz.q: A request arrives with a known idempotency key but a different amount than the stored one. What should the API do?
options: Return the stored response for the old amount
Process it as a new charge
Reject it as a key conflict
Silently overwrite the stored record
quiz.why: The same key must mean the same intent. A different payload signals a client bug or misuse, and guessing could charge the wrong amount or hide the error.

quiz.q: Why is PUT /users/42 with name set to Ana naturally idempotent while POST /charges is not?
options: PUT is faster
Repeating PUT sets the same final state, while each POST creates a new record
PUT is encrypted
POST cannot be retried
quiz.why: Setting a resource to a fixed value gives the same state no matter how many times it runs. Creating a new record each call changes state every time, so it needs a key.

cheatsheet.def: Applying it N times leaves the system in the same state as applying it once. Setting a value is idempotent; incrementing a counter is not.
A client-generated unique ID (such as a UUID) sent with every attempt of one logical action so the server can recognise repeats.
Storage of seen keys or message IDs, often with the saved response, protected by a unique constraint. Usually has a TTL such as 24 hours.
The sender retries until acknowledged, so a message may arrive more than once but is never silently lost. The common broker default.
Not exactly-once delivery. It is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer that commits its dedup record atomically with the side effect.
Insert the key under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect. Avoid check-then-act, which races under concurrency.
Store a hash of the request with the key. Same key with a different payload is an error, not a replay.
Designing operations as 'set X to V' or 'upsert by ID' so repeats are harmless without any key table.
